# Climate Intervention and Mitigation: Strategic Responses to Technological Advances in Solar Geoengineering

- Open access
- Published: 24 March 2026

- Todd L. Cherry 1, 2, 
- Stephan Kroll 3 & 
- David M. McEvoy ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0001-7466-3681 4 

## Abstract

The urgency of addressing climate change has led to the exploration of solar geoengineering (SGE)—a collection of technologies that cool the planet by reflecting a fraction of sunlight back into space. One of the most prominent concerns with SGE is that it may crowd out greenhouse gas mitigation efforts. This paper examines how advances in SGE technologies may impact mitigation. We conduct a social dilemma experiment with treatments that vary how effective SGE is at reducing climate damages and the level of certainty about its effects. Results indicate SGE generally leads to increased cooperation on mitigation, but importantly, we find that mitigation levels decrease significantly as SGE technologies become more effective and less uncertain. At an individual level, agents that stand to benefit the most tend to decrease mitigation, while those that are vulnerable to SGE act to diminish the role of SGE by increasing mitigation.

## 1 Introduction

Driving down greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions is the necessary long-term solution to climate change, but the window is closing for emission reductions alone to avoid the potential tipping points and catastrophic impacts from climate change. In response, researchers and policymakers have begun to consider emerging technologies that intervene in the climate system to limit or temporarily reverse anthropogenic climate change. Solar geoengineering (SGE)—a large-scale intervention to cool the planet by managing the amount of solar radiation that reaches earth—has emerged as the leading candidate because it is feasible with existing technologies and could be implemented in a short period of time at a relatively low cost (Nordhaus 1994; Barrett 2008; Smith 2020; Smith et al. 2024). However, uncertainties exist about the efficacy and side effects of SGE as well as the possible impacts on climate cooperation and governance (Aldy et al. 2021; Harding et al. 2023; Vattioni et al. 2025).

A growing literature has begun to examine the social complexities, strategic implications, and governance challenges of SGE. One prominent concern is that the emergence of SGE may weaken the resolve for reducing GHG emissions, commonly referred to as “moral hazard” but more accurately described as crowding out or mitigation deterrence (Keith 2000, Reynolds 2019; Tsipiras and Grant 2022; Wagner and Zizzamia 2022). Social scientists have recently intensified their research on the question of whether SGE might crowd out mitigation efforts. Most empirical studies have relied on surveys and incentivized experiments. The survey evidence points to SGE having no effect on mitigation (Fairbrother 2016; Merk et al. 2019; Austin and Converse 2021) or the opposite effect in which SGE motivates an increased concern and willingness to cooperate on climate action (Kahan et al. 2015; Merk et al. 2016; Cherry et al. 2021). The only survey study finding that SGE weakened resolve to mitigate emissions is Raimi et al. (2019), and their result is conditional on framing SGE as having the potential to be a major solution to climate change.

A limitation of surveys is that they fail to capture the collective-action challenge that defines the climate change dilemma. While isolated responses to surveys may reflect individual preferences, they do not shed light on the important strategic interactions that matter to the question of moral hazard (Moreno-Cruz 2015). To better understand the strategic interactions between SGE and mitigation, recent studies have turned to social dilemma experiments that consider both the individual and collective channels. The few incentivized experimental studies (Andrews et al. 2022; Cherry et al. 2023a, b, 2024) largely find that SGE has either no effect on mitigation or acts as a call to action that crowds in mitigation (i.e., reverse moral hazard). However, the results are based on a fixed set of parameters that define the efficacy of SGE when the potential for SGE to crowd out mitigation likely depends on the characteristics of the technology. The existing evidence therefore offers little insight on the cause-and-effect relationships that determine the strategic responses to SGE. Our study addresses this issue by investigating how two key features of SGE determine whether the technology is likely to crowd in or out mitigation efforts: (i) the level of effectiveness that SGE protects against climate change damages and (ii) the level of risk of the outcomes from SGE deployment.

Our approach uses a similar baseline theoretical and experimental setting as in Cherry et al. (2023a) and expands it by varying the effectiveness and risk levels of SGE technologies. Following the growing literature using theory and experiments to analyze behavior and decision-making in the context of climate change (Milinski et al. 2008; Dannenberg and Barrett 2012; Abatayo et al. 2020), our experiments capture the important tensions and incentives that characterize the underlying social dilemma. While a variety of different SGE technologies exists, we use the features of stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) as motivation for our theoretical and experimental framework because of its potential global impact and relatively low deployment cost. Following the literature on SAI, we characterize SGE as inexpensive and imperfect with agents preferring different levels of deployment that depend on mitigation; thereby creating a tension between the socially optimal level of deployment and the theoretically predicted free-driver outcome of excessive SGE deployment (Wagner and Weitzman 2012).

Whereas Cherry et al. (2023a) investigated the moral-hazard conjecture with players making both mitigation and SGE deployment decisions, we simplify the design to focus on how the features of SGE affect mitigation decisions. In our design, the overall SGE level is automatically set at the theoretically predicted level; that is, SGE is deployed at the highest preferred level. The experiment therefore imposes the “free driver” outcome (Weitzman 2015) in the second stage and focuses on the mitigation decisions in the first stage. Importantly, the realized SGE level in the second stage is determined by the group’s total investment in mitigation in the first stage—greater mitigation lowers the free-driver’s preferred level and thus lowers the deployment of SGE.

The novel contribution of our paper is that we consider how two characteristics of SGE impact the level of investment in mitigation: the effectiveness of SGE and the risk of SGE outcomes. The level of effectiveness is defined as the fraction of damages avoided by SGE deployment and is different for different group members. Lower SGE effectiveness avoids a smaller fraction of damages. The level of risk, which is motivated by the fact that the exact impact of SGE is unknown, is defined as the range of possible outcomes from SGE deployment. Lower risk has a smaller range of possible SGE effectiveness. The experimental design exogenously varies effectiveness and risk to identify causal effects on mitigation.

At the aggregate level, results add to the experimental and survey evidence that the introduction of SGE may lead to greater investment in mitigation. However, findings offer new insights on how SGE and mitigation may co-evolve over time. Specifically, our study provides theoretical and empirical evidence indicating that investment in mitigation will fall as research and development lead to improvements in SGE technology over time. Thus, as SGE becomes a better substitute for mitigation, we should expect less mitigation. The analysis also examines the individual strategic behavior and finds competing strategic responses to SGE, with those that benefit the most from SGE reducing mitigation and those vulnerable to SGE increasing mitigation, in part, to diminish the position of the free driver.

The next section introduces two mitigation games, one in which players can protect themselves from climate damages using only mitigation, and another in which players can, in addition to mitigation, also deploy solar geoengineering to partially protect themselves from climate damages. The third section describes the experiments used to test the implications of the games, focusing on the impacts of varying both, the effectiveness of solar geoengineering technologies and the level of risk. The fourth section presents the results from the experiments and tests of the predictions. We conclude in the final section.

## 2 The Games

Following Cherry et al. (2023a), we consider a baseline game in which \(\:n\) players in a group face the possibility of suffering financial losses from an impending disaster (akin to climate change damages). Players start with two accounts with initial monetary balances. A spending account can be used to make investments to protect against the disaster (i.e., mitigation), and a savings account that cannot be accessed and represents wealth. If no investment is undertaken, spending balances stay intact, but the impending disaster will eliminate all players’ savings balances. The final payoff is determined by the sum of spending and savings balances, with equal weights.

The players can invest units from their spending account into a public account, which helps reduce the losses of units in the savings accounts (the mitigation decision). Each unit invested in mitigation by any player protects \(\:\sigma\:\) units of savings for all players, with a marginal return \(\:0<\sigma\:<1\), which implies that an individual player is financially worse off investing in mitigation. An additional assumption \(\:n\sigma\:>1\) implies that collectively the group is strictly better off the more units that are invested in mitigation. Thus, the baseline game is a traditional social dilemma, and the Nash equilibrium is no investment in mitigation. The social optimum, however, requires players to fully invest their total spending balance in mitigation.

The payoff function for player i in the baseline game is

$$\:{\pi}_{i}=\left(G-{m}_{i}\right)+R-\left(R-\:\sigma{M}\right),$$

 (1) 

where \(\:G\) denotes the starting balance in the spending account, \(\:{m}_{i}\) is player i’s investment into mitigation, \(\:R\) is the starting balance in the savings account, and \(\:M=\sum\:_{i=1}^{n}{m}_{i}\). We impose the additional assumption \(\:\sigma\:M<R\) for all players, which means that it is not possible for the group to completely protect their savings, even in the social optimum in which all players fully invest their spending accounts. This broadly reflects that global mitigation objectives outside of the lab are also focused on damage reduction, not elimination, as illustrated, for example, by the Paris Agreement target of 1.5 degree warming relative to pre-industrial levels.

The payoff equation in the baseline game can be simplified to

$$\:{\pi}_{i}=(G-{m}_{i})+\sigma{M}.$$

The Nash equilibrium payoff is \(\:{\pi\:}_{i}^{NE}=G\) for all n players (i.e., \(\:{m}_{i}\) = 0 for all i), and the social optimum payoff is \(\:{\pi\:}_{i}^{*}=\sigma\:nG\) (i.e., \(\:{m}_{i}\) = \(\:G\) for all i).

### 2.1 Solar Geoengineering

A new technology – solar geoengineering (SGE) – is now available that can help players protect some of their savings; the game has two stages.
